parts.title: Booking a blood donation
parts.context: A young man books his first blood donation.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a young man phoning a blood donation service to book an appointment. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: National Blood Service, Karen speaking.

script.speaker: joe
script.text: Hello. I'd like to book an appointment to give blood, please. I've never done it before.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: That's wonderful. Everyone remembers their first time. I'll take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: It is the caller's first donation, so 'first' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: joe
script.text: Joe Lawson. That's L-A-W-S-O-N.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Thank you, Joe. How old are you? You need to be at least seventeen.

script.speaker: joe
script.text: I'm nineteen.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Good. And a quick question about your weight. You need to weigh at least fifty kilos.

script.speaker: joe
script.text: I'm well over that. I weigh about seventy.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Have you had any tattoos or piercings recently?

script.speaker: joe
script.text: I had a tattoo five months ago. Is that a problem?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: No, you have to wait four months, so you're fine. When would you like to come?

script.speaker: joe
script.text: Thursday, if possible. I'm free after lectures.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: We have a session on Thursday at four o'clock. There's also one at six, but that's usually full.

script.speaker: joe
script.text: Four is perfect. Where is it?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: At the Memorial Hall, on Church Street. It's next to the library, and you can't miss it, because of the big red banner.

script.speaker: joe
script.text: Is there anything I should do beforehand?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Yes, it's important to eat a good meal in the two hours before you come. People who haven't eaten are more likely to feel faint. And drink plenty of water, at least half a litre, as that makes it easier to find a vein.

script.speaker: joe
script.text: How long will it take?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: The donation itself takes about ten minutes, but you should allow an hour for the whole visit, because there's a short health check first, and a rest and a drink afterwards.

script.speaker: joe
script.text: And will I be able to go to a lecture afterwards?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Yes, but please avoid heavy exercise for the rest of the day. We'll see you on Thursday, Joe. And thank you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A village flower show
parts.context: An organiser briefs volunteers at a flower show.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear an organiser welcoming volunteers to a village flower show. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: cole
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for helping at this year's flower show. I'm Peter Cole, the chairman. Please look at the plan of the show ground. We're at the main gate, at the bottom, and the path runs straight ahead to the bandstand, at the top in the middle.

script.speaker: cole
script.text: On the left of the path, the tent nearest the gate is the children's activity area, where there are painting and planting for the younger visitors. Above it, in the middle on the left, is the floral art marquee. And at the top on the left is the rose marquee, which is the most popular, so you'll need two stewards there.

script.speaker: cole
script.text: On the right, the nearest to the gate is the refreshment tent. Above it, in the middle, is the plant sales area, where local nurseries sell their plants. And at the top on the right is the vegetable tent, with the giant marrows and onions.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: cole
script.text: Some facts for you. The show is a hundred and fifty years old this year. The first one was held in a farmer's field with just thirty entries, and now we have more than eight hundred.

script.speaker: cole
script.text: We're expecting about five thousand visitors, which is a record. The weather forecast is good, but please be ready to direct people to the covered areas if it rains.

script.speaker: cole
script.text: The prize for best in show is a silver cup, which has been awarded since the very first show. There's also a cash prize of fifty pounds for the best vegetable display.

script.speaker: cole
script.text: Dogs are not allowed in the marquees, except for assistance dogs. Please tell visitors politely. There's a dog-sitting area by the gate, run by the scouts.

script.speaker: cole
script.text: The prize-giving is at three o'clock at the bandstand. Please make sure the area is clear by half past two, so the judges can set up. Thank you all, and have a wonderful day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Designing a library chatbot
parts.context: Two computer science students write up a chatbot project.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two computer science students, Ines and Will, discussing a chatbot for a university library. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: ines
script.text: Will, shall we go through the design of our chatbot before we write it up?

script.speaker: will
script.text: Sure. The purpose is to answer the common questions that students ask the library, like opening hours and how to renew a book.

script.speaker: ines
script.text: Right. And we chose a simple design, because we only had eight weeks, and a more advanced system would never have been finished.

script.speaker: will
script.text: True. What was the biggest problem when we tested it?

script.speaker: ines
script.text: That students ask unexpected questions. People don't type what you expect. They use slang, and they make spelling mistakes.

script.speaker: will
script.text: How many test questions did we collect?

script.speaker: ines
script.text: A hundred and twenty, from the library staff and from students on the course.

script.speaker: will
script.text: And how many did the chatbot answer correctly?

script.speaker: ines
script.text: About eighty percent, which isn't bad, but the library wanted ninety, so we need to say what we would improve.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: ines
script.text: Now let me describe how it works, step by step. First, the user types a question into the window on the library website.

script.speaker: will
script.text: Then the program looks for keywords in the question, such as 'renew' or 'opening'.

script.speaker: ines
script.text: It searches a database of previous questions and answers, and finds the ones with the same keywords.

script.speaker: will
script.text: Each possible answer is given a score, depending on how many keywords match, and the highest score wins.

script.speaker: ines
script.text: And if no answer scores high enough, the question is passed to a human librarian, who replies by email.

script.speaker: will
script.text: That's a good safety net. I think the diagram will make it clear.

script.speaker: ines
script.text: I'll draw it tonight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the development of the telephone
parts.context: A lecture on the history of the telephone.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the development of the telephone. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about the telephone, which in little more than a century has changed from a scientific curiosity to something that almost everyone carries in a pocket.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The telephone was patented in eighteen seventy-six by Alexander Graham Bell, though other inventors were working on similar ideas, and there are still arguments about who deserves the credit. According to Bell's own notes, the first words ever spoken on a telephone were to his assistant, Thomas Watson, in the next room: Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In the early days, there was no direct dialling. Each call had to be connected by a human operator, who sat at a switchboard and plugged cables into sockets to link the two people. The first telephone exchange opened in eighteen seventy-eight, and by the end of the century, there were hundreds of thousands of phones.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The quality of the early telephones was poor. Thomas Edison made a major improvement by inventing a better microphone, which made voices much louder and clearer.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Long distance was the next challenge. The first telephone cable across the Atlantic Ocean was laid in nineteen fifty-six, and it carried only a few dozen calls at once. Today, calls are carried by fibre-optic cables, which can handle millions, and by satellites.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The most dramatic change was the mobile phone. The first call from a handheld mobile was made in nineteen seventy-three by Martin Cooper, an engineer at Motorola. The phone weighed about a kilogram, and it took ten hours to charge, and it gave you only half an hour of talking.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The first text message was sent in nineteen ninety-two. It was just two words: Merry Christmas. And then, in two thousand and seven, the first modern smartphone appeared, combining a phone, a camera and a computer in one device. Next week we'll look at the history of the internet.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
